Latvian Exporters Face Uncertainty as Turkey Imposes Sweeping Import Tariffs

Latvian exporters are grappling with a sudden downturn in foreign demand as Turkey’s newly imposed blanket tariffs on a broad range of Latvian goods continue to disrupt trade flows. The tariffs, announced last month and effective immediately, target over 300 product categories, including timber, machinery, processed foods, and textiles—sectors that form the backbone of Latvia’s export economy.

According to the Latvian Ministry of Economics, the value of goods affected by the Turkish tariffs in 2023 amounted to more than €420 million, representing nearly 8% of Latvia’s total exports. “We are seeing a direct impact on our manufacturing and agricultural sectors,” said Deputy Minister Ilze Kļaviņa in a press briefing on Thursday. “Many small and medium-sized exporters have shipments held at Turkish customs, and contractual negotiations are stalling.”

The Turkish Ministry of Trade cited the need to “rebalance trade relations and address structural imbalances” for the measure, but Latvian officials say the move is disproportionate and threatens livelihoods. “We hope for a swift resolution through diplomatic channels, but right now our members are facing significant losses and mounting uncertainty,” said Janis Ozols, head of the Latvian Exporters’ Association.

Local producers such as Baltic Timberworks and RigaFoods are reporting a 40% dip in monthly orders from Turkish clients. The Confederation of Latvian Industries estimates that up to 2,500 jobs could be at risk if the tariffs persist through the end of the year.

Economist Dace Jansone from the University of Latvia warned, “The knock-on effects could be substantial, affecting supply chains and investment decisions across the region.” While the government is exploring alternative markets and support measures, industry associations stress that a quick diplomatic solution is crucial to prevent further losses.

As talks between Riga and Ankara continue, Latvian exporters are bracing for continued disruption in one of their key non-EU markets.
